articles.title: Op-Ed: Stop MAGA from Taking Over Washington, Vote No on I-645, I-001, and I-638
articles.author: Suresh Chanmugam
paras: I was born and raised in Baton Rouge, Louisiana to immigrant parents. I moved to Seattle in 1999 to work as a software engineer in large part due to the progressive values cultivated by Washington State. My wife and I are grateful to the communities and culture here, where we’ve been able to raise three children who attend public schools in diverse communities. One of the reasons we are raising our kids here is Washington’s commitment to inclusion. Our state was one of the first to pass marriage equality, and we have strong laws against discrimination.

I deeply appreciate that the tech industry in Washington is considered a safe, welcoming place for LGBTQIA+ people, particularly our transgender friends and colleagues, who face escalating threats to their very right to existence. More parents, including many of our tech colleagues, say they are moving here to protect their children from draconian laws that are linked to increases in suicide rates.

But, near-trillionaire Elon Musk is fanning the flames against the transgender community by spending hundreds of millions of dollars through his “America PAC” (political action committee) running anti-trans political ads in elections around the country to try to drive swing voters to vote Republican. Most voters agree that this strategy is using hate to try to distract us from the high cost of groceries, gas, housing, and healthcare.

Now, right here in blue Washington State, multi-millionaire hedge fund manager Brian Heywood, through his PAC Let’s Go Washington, is using the same MAGA playbook. Heywood and his posse of right-wing uber rich supporters are bankrolling three harmful ballot measures before Washington voters this election, and two of them put a target on the backs of LGBTQIA+ children, a particularly malicious tactic.

Initiative 638 (IL26-638 on your ballot) is the most extreme policy of its kind in the country, and that’s saying a lot when red states like Idaho, Florida, Tennessee, Kansas, Utah, and Iowa have passed dozens of laws restricting civil rights, freedoms and access to care for transgender people. To exclude and humiliate trans girls from sports, I-638 would require all girls to undergo sex inspections to play elementary, middle, or high school sports.

Doctors say to be in compliance with this new rule, they will have to conduct invasive genital exams on young girls or expensive genetic and hormone testing that is unlikely to be covered by insurance because it is not medically-necessary. (And in blatant discrimination, only girls would be required to undergo potentially harmful sex inspections because the initiative exempts boys.)

Initiative 001 (IL26-001) is an anti-parents rights, anti-LGBTQIA+ measure. As a parent of three Seattle Public Schools teenagers, I know the facts: parents already have the right to information about their child, including the right to opt them out of certain curriculum or programs, and to talk to teachers, school counselors or nurses about their concerns.

While most kids have a safe loving home, sadly not all do. There were more than 115,000 reports of child abuse in Washington state in 2024 alone. As someone deeply involved with work to address our housing crisis, I have seen that the majority of homeless youth are LGBTQIA+ kids who have been kicked out or left their home because they didn’t feel safe there. I-001 will make this crisis worse, and is a direct threat to the safety of vulnerable young children who need confidential access to trusted, trained professionals like school counselors.

Initiative 645 (IP26-645) is an extension of Musk and the billionaire bros who successfully lobbied the Trump administration for policies that benefit themselves, Heywood is also trying to buy a tax cut for himself and other extremely wealthy individuals by repealing Washington’s new millionaires tax. The tax itself is very popular with the majority of voters in part because it pays for B&O tax cuts for small businesses (including small tech startups) and cuts the regressive sales taxes that impact working families. It raises billions for schools, childcare, free meals for K-12 students, and tax rebates for working families.

Having grown up in Louisiana, a state notorious for underfunded public schools, it’s appalling to me that Washington’s public school system isn’t much better. Our schools are chronically underfunded due to our state’s upside down tax code and I-645 will make it worse.

I’m tired of the false narrative that workers and businesses are leaving the state because of the millionaires tax. Skilled workers don’t want to leave Washington and move to Tennessee or Texas where they could face jail time and even death because they had a miscarriage. In fact, Starbucks, Oracle, and others have struggled to convince their employees to leave Washington. Over 100 Seattle Starbucks employees chose to have their job eliminated rather than move their family to a red state. Oracle moved its headquarters to Nashville and added only seven net new employees there last year. Austin is declining as a tech hub.

The Seattle metro region is the second largest tech hub in the country, but passing these initiatives would risk a tech talent flight to communities with stronger human rights protections like the Bay Area, New York City, Boston, and Northern Virginia. Political initiatives like I-645, I-001, and I-638 aren't just harmful to marginalized members of our community; they're also bad for business.

I urge my tech colleagues to say no to Brian Heywood and his attempt to distract us from the real problems caused by MAGA politicians, like exorbitant groceries, escalating rents, disappearing health care, and a reckless war that has killed innocent civilians and caused permanent destruction of business data that was supposed to have 99.999999999% (11 nines) of durability . Rejecting Heywood’s initiatives is one way we can protect all children’s rights, health, safety, educational, and economic opportunities.
Suresh Chanmugam has worked as a software engineer in Seattle since 1999 and is a steering committee member of Tech 4 Housing .
Editor's note: The Urbanist Elections Committee also endorsed a "no" vote on Initiatives 001, 638, and 645 .

articles.title: PONGO POETRY | when will i drop?
paras: by a young person at the Echo Glen Children’s Center
do you love me or do you hate me? like a rose there is a gorgeous side and a bad side bright like the red petals but ugly like the spiky thorn
every day that my petals fall i wonder when they're all gonna drop blooming into birth of promised death
when will be my last day sitting in the sun and standing in the rain? when the sun goes away i can't sleep but when the sun comes back my growth continues growing with death on my mind
if i lost all of my petals of life would everybody look at me the same or would they step all over my roots?
by a young person at the Echo Glen Children’s Center
Like an animal in a zoo imprisoned, scared, sad, lonely too like an animal in a zoo. this is just my point of view I've got feelings too.
I miss my mom I miss my dad I'm hurting so bad
but it's ok I'm writing a poem about my lifestyle. tell me how I'm supposed to be I tried loving, healing, but you took it all away from me.
by a young person at the Echo Glen Children’s Center

I used to think freedom was being able to do, say what you wanted, and go whenever you wanted. I used to think I wouldn't be able to be free until I no longer had to press a button to use the bathroom. Ask for doors to be unlocked or finally having a choice in what food I ate. I was wrong in so many ways. I discovered freedom when I let go of the rope connected to all my anger. When I finally let go and allowed the burns to heal. I discovered freedom when I didn't allow the pain I hid to continue to drown me in silence. When I finally came up for air. I discovered freedom when I unlocked the shackles bonded by childhood trauma When I finally allowed the weight to disappear. When I finally allowed my wings to spread mentally When I allowed my mind to soar. So while I'm still physically behind these walls and confined in these buildings. I'm as free as ever. I've learned freedom is a mindset and that mindset is something that no one can ever take away. I've finally set myself free.

Pongo Poetry Project's mission is to engage youth in writing poetry to inspire healing and growth. The Echo Glen Children's Center, a juvenile institution for youth serving criminal sentences, is one of Pongo's flagship program sites in the Seattle area. Studies of incarcerated youth indicate that up to 70% suffer from a mental health disorder and that many have experienced childhood trauma. Youth at Echo Glen have endured significant mental and emotional challenges in the last two years, including increased rates of depression, anxiety, sleep issues, and behavioral challenges.

Pongo believes there is power in creative expression, and articulating one’s pain to an empathetic audience. Through this special monthly column in partnership with the South Seattle Emerald, Pongo invites readers to bear witness to the pain, resilience, and creative capacity of youth whose voices and perspectives are too often relegated to the periphery. To learn more about Pongo’s work of inspiring healing and relief among youth coping with mental and emotional turmoil, register for its upcoming event , Envisioning Voices, on Dec. 10.

articles.title: Exit interview: Microsoft’s comms chief on CEOs, reporters, what he got wrong, and stories that stuck
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The name Frank X. Shaw isn’t as well known outside the company as those of Microsoft’s other senior leaders, and that’s the nature of the job. But behind the scenes, the company’s longtime communications chief has shaped its public image for nearly three decades, working for all three of its CEOs and handling its biggest stories along the way, from antitrust to AI.

Shaw announced in September that he’s leaving Microsoft at the end of the year. On this week’s GeekWire Podcast, he sits down for what amounts to an exit interview. We’re joined in the conversation by longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley , editor in chief of Directions on Microsoft and a GeekWire contributing writer.

Shaw talks candidly about working for Bill Gates, Steve Ballmer and Satya Nadella, and about the situations he’d handle differently. He describes his behind-the-scenes dealings with some of the top reporters in tech, from an executive’s objection to a single word to the heated argument that changed how he saw his job.
He also reflects on how communications and media are changing in the AI era, and explains why trust still comes down to a belief in the person telling the story.
Listen below, and continue reading for highlights.
On Microsoft’s three CEOs: Shaw says intensity is what the three have in common, expressed differently: “Steve was outwardly intense. Satya is quietly intense, and Bill is cuttingly intense.”

Ballmer was the hardest to explain to the public, he says, because the loud-salesman caricature hid a thoughtful, detail-oriented leader who often played the boisterous public role because Microsoft’s sales force needed it.

On the clarity of hindsight: Big decisions look obvious once they work out, Shaw says. His example is the board’s choice of Satya Nadella as CEO. It’s seen as a no-brainer now, but at the time there was a lot of debate, there were other candidates, and it was a hard, complicated decision.
“When you get a decision right, it always looks easy afterwards,” he says. “If you get it wrong, you were just an idiot all along.”
On speaking up: A communications leader should weigh in when a decision could damage the brand, Shaw says, and he learned that the hard way.

When Mary Jo asks how he decides when to push back on executives, she raises the Kin as an example. Shaw says he thought the phone would fail. It was late to market, and it would cost more than people expected because it required a data plan. Engineers he talked to had their doubts, too.
But when Ballmer went around the table asking whether to launch it, Shaw stayed quiet, unsure a communications executive had standing to weigh in. Microsoft pulled it within weeks.

In hindsight, he says, framing it as a brand risk would have given him standing to speak: if the Kin failed, it would cause significant brand damage and hurt Microsoft with the younger audience it was trying to reach. He doubts speaking up would have changed the decision, but says he would have felt better about it.
On underestimating a story: A story that doesn’t get much initial attention can still define a company for years. Shaw’s example: Vanity Fair’s 2012 “lost decade” story .

As he recounts it, reporter Kurt Eichenwald told him, “If you don’t give me Steve and Bill, I’m just going to write a hit piece,” and then did. Shaw says he should have escalated to Vanity Fair sooner, and he underestimated how a story that got little immediate pickup would shape how reporters described Microsoft for the next four years.

On narratives: Continuing on that theme, Shaw says facts can be disputed but “narratives are sticky,” and a company can only change one by changing its own behavior. In the 2000s, he says, every story described Microsoft as “a convicted monopolist,” and ending stack ranking was part of how the company moved past the lost-decade image.

On what makes a good story: Shaw recalls having a shouting match with Rob Guth, then a Wall Street Journal reporter, over an article Shaw no longer remembers. It got heated enough that Shaw pulled his car over in Madison Park to keep arguing. (Guth now works as a writer and researcher for Bill Gates.)

Guth told him he was bad at his job because he thought the job was getting positive stories. What Shaw should want, Guth said, were interesting stories that showed something real about the company. Some would be less flattering, but they would be more memorable.

Shaw told him he was wrong. But after thinking it over, he concluded Guth was exactly right. A story about a product built perfectly that everyone loves is boring, he says. “That’s like the plane landed safely. Nobody cares.” The coverage worth hoping for illuminates part of the company in a memorable way, and that always comes with tension.

On taking risks with reporters: Cooperating on a story you can’t control is a risk worth taking when the result shows something real about the company, Shaw says. Asked by Mary Jo for an example, he points to The New Yorker’s long piece on Microsoft’s relationship with OpenAI, featuring Kevin Scott, the Microsoft chief technology officer.

Microsoft agreed to it knowing that the writer, Charles Duhigg, would talk to many people and test a thesis along the way, so there was no telling what would come out. Then Sam Altman’s brief ouster from OpenAI happened right before the story went to press. It was a risky story, Shaw says, but it captured the company at a revealing moment.
On corrections: Shaw’s test is whether something is “irritating” or “damaging.” Only factual errors that matter are worth pursuing, he says.

His example is a Bloomberg story by Dina Bass that described an executive as having “wooed” customers. The executive hated the word and wanted it changed, so Shaw made what he calls the run up the hill, pressing Bass on the exec’s behalf and asking her to check with her editors.
She pointed out that she hadn’t quoted the executive using the word, and the editors left it alone. The executive didn’t like it, Shaw says, but it wasn’t wrong.
On speaking with one voice: Shaw says a big part of his job was trying to ensure that a company of Microsoft’s size made sense to the world.

He recalls a Seattle Times reporter who got 26 pitches from Microsoft in one week and asked him which ones Microsoft thought were important. Sending pitches indiscriminately was a mistake, he says. The company needed to decide what three or four things mattered most and focus its messaging on those.

On building in public: Asked about recent internal memos pointing Microsoft toward more voices and less central messaging as he departs, Shaw says the company already has many employees talking about its products on LinkedIn, X and Reddit, and that’s a good thing.

Someone from Microsoft answering questions in a Reddit Excel thread doesn’t need to be babysat by the communications team, he says. He sees it as a continuation of what Microsoft did with Channel 9 and thousands of MSDN blogs.
At the same time, he says, there are moments, such as a big event or a major launch, when the company needs to break through.

“Every once in a while you want the world to know Microsoft had something to say today,” he says. That’s hard, it takes real effort, and it can’t happen every week or even every month, so the company has to pick those moments and do them right.

On AI and the media: AI can help spokespeople prepare, Shaw says, but asking it what Mary Jo will ask, for example, produces “generic Mary Jo questions.” The best interviewers, he says, deliberately avoid the predictable question.

On reporters’ styles: Preparing a spokesperson means knowing how a particular reporter works, Shaw says, and that comes from people who have sat through many of their interviews. His example is Steven Levy, the veteran tech journalist and Wired editor at large, who Shaw says can lull you with 10 minutes of easygoing conversation, then hit you with one sharp question after another.
Other reporters always sound negative in interviews but write straightforward stories, he says, and an executive who reads too much into the tone risks getting knocked off their game.

Asked to name the toughest reporter he has dealt with, Shaw pushes back on the label. Good reporters are tricky to work with because their job is to find things out and surprise you with what they know, he says. That doesn’t make them tough. What makes a situation difficult is usually a story with real conflict and tension, not the reporter.

On Microsoft in the AI era: Shaw sees AI in a transitional moment, moving away from a constant focus on the models themselves. Right now, he says, every new model release or manifesto makes everyone stop and look.
He hopes the attention will shift from new models to whether AI is actually useful, and he says that’s where Microsoft has historically been strongest.

Acknowledging that he’s still on the payroll and rooting for the company, he offers an analogy that will resonate with anyone who learned to drive a stick shift. The AI model companies want to drop a bigger, more powerful engine into businesses, and the result is often a lot of grinding of gears.
“We’re the clutch,” he says. Microsoft’s infrastructure, in his telling, lets companies absorb that power and get moving without the disruption of a new engine and a demand to go 110 miles per hour.

On journalism: “People trust what they hear because they trust the people,” Shaw says. Deep knowledge of a beat becomes more valuable as the world gets more transactional, he says, even as the business behind it becomes less sustainable.

On what’s next: Shaw plans to take some time off and isn’t making any big decisions. People have suggested consulting, another big communications job or board seats, he says, but he doesn’t want to rush into anything.

articles.title: Amazon ends its six-year legal fight with former AWS managers over alleged data center kickbacks
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Two former Amazon real estate managers acknowledged receiving personal payments tied to data center deals they handled for the company, under a settlement that resolves the company’s claims against them in a six-year lawsuit.

Carl Nelson and Casey Kirschner “regret their actions, apologize for failing to meet Amazon’s high ethical standards, and are glad this matter has been resolved,” according to a joint statement that the parties agreed to as part of the settlement.

The payments “violated Amazon’s Code of Conduct & Ethics, broke the trust Amazon places in its employees, and put Amazon’s reputation at risk in the communities it serves,” says the statement, which Amazon provided Friday evening in response to GeekWire’s inquiry.

The statement doesn’t call the payments kickbacks or say they were illegal. Nelson was investigated by the FBI but never charged, and a federal judge ruled in 2023 that Amazon’s Code of Conduct wasn’t a legally enforceable contract. The other terms of the settlement are confidential, including whether any money changed hands.
Before the settlement, Nelson had maintained that he abided by the terms of his Amazon employment agreement, which his attorneys said gave him broad leeway to do outside business.
Rodney Atherton, a Colorado attorney who set up business entities for the two men, also settled and “regrets the role he played in the conduct at issue in this case,” according to the statement.

The settlement closes a long legal ordeal for Nelson’s family. His wife, Amy Nelson, the former Seattle entrepreneur who founded The Riveter, a network of co-working spaces for women, has been his most outspoken advocate, defending him for years on social media and in interviews and criticizing Amazon and the Justice Department for pursuing him.
“All disputes with my husband’s former employer have been resolved,” she said in a short video posted Friday on social media.
The case upended the family’s life. The FBI seized $892,135 from the Nelsons’ bank accounts in 2020, including hundreds of thousands of dollars Amy Nelson earned as CEO of The Riveter.

The government returned most of it in a 2022 settlement. By then, the Nelsons had sold their West Seattle home and emptied their retirement accounts to pay lawyers, and they had moved with their four daughters to Hawaii and then Ohio, where Amy’s parents live. The family had spent more than $3 million on legal fees, she told KIRO 7 in 2023.

“Many of the things that we lost over the past four years, we can never get back. We can never get our home back. We can never get our jobs back. We can never get our reputation back,” she told The Seattle Times in 2024, after federal prosecutors moved to drop the related criminal cases.
Amazon told the judge on Oct. 20 that it had reached the settlement, less than two weeks before the case was set to go to trial in U.S. District Court in Alexandria, Va., according to court filings.

The case continues against the remaining defendants, Brian Watson and his Denver-based real estate firm, Northstar Commercial Partners, which Amazon hired for nine data center development projects in Northern Virginia between 2018 and 2020. Amazon alleges that Northstar won that business by paying kickbacks to Nelson and Kirschner, which Watson denies.
Watson and Northstar are headed to trial Nov. 2. In a filing Friday, they asked the judge to make Amazon hand over the settlement agreement so they can see its terms.

The settlement follows years of rulings that went both ways. In April 2023, a federal judge dismissed most of Amazon’s claims , including its breach of contract claims against Nelson and Kirschner. In September 2025, a federal appeals court revived several of the claims , including racketeering and fraud, and sent the case back for trial.

In January 2024, federal prosecutors moved to vacate the guilty pleas of two other men in the case, Kirschner’s brother, Christian Kirschner, and former Northstar account manager Kyle Ramstetter, calling prosecution “not in the best interests of justice.”
Prosecutors added that they had declined to prosecute the other alleged co-conspirators, including Nelson.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Prop 1 Will Sustain Seattle's Transit Momentum
articles.author: Ashwin Bhumbla
paras: It cost me three dollars to get to City Hall the day I joined many others to fight for the future of Seattle transit. An Uber would have been a little faster but much more expensive at twenty dollars. I could've used a Lime bike, but it would've taken longer and, again, would have been more expensive at around fifteen dollars. Maybe I could've driven, but like 20% of households in Seattle , I don't own a car. I shudder to think how much purchasing one for that drive would've set me back.

So, I left the cafe I was working from and despite having recently missed a bus, I had to wait only seven minutes until the next one arrived. I hopped on the Route 7 and in about twenty minutes I was at City Hall along with dozens of others to advocate for a strong Seattle Transit Measure renewal in front of City Council . The trip was affordable, safe, fast, and easy.

After listening to over an hour of public testimony, it was clear that transit advocacy was only scratching the surface of reasons folks relied on the bus. I heard workers in tech, healthcare, service, public works, manufacturing, and trade describe the route they relied on to get to work. I heard seniors who could not afford to or who were unable to drive speak glowingly of the bus that took them to groceries, healthcare visits, and to resource centers. I heard union workers speak to what working for the transit system meant to them and their families. Speaker after speaker remarked on how they would not be able to afford to get to the places they needed to go without the bus. Finally, I heard a commenter describe how they relied on the bus for love, taking it to a first date – drawing the loudest cheer from the crowd of the day.

The advocacy that day succeeded. The measure we were fighting for survived being watered down and is now on your ballots. For a more affordable, sustainable, and accessible city, and for every person, I heard that day, and in the many days since, I’m voting yes on Proposition 1 to renew the Seattle Transit Measure and to expand and improve our incredible transit system.

Before asking you to do the same, perhaps some background context would be helpful. The Seattle Transit Measure (STM) renewal will authorize the city to collect a 0.3% sales tax for 10 years, collecting approximately $138 million annually. This is an increase from the current STM which is a six year sales tax (2020 to 2026) at a 0.15% sales tax rate, generating around $50 million annually. These funds will be spent on a variety of transit-related investments, but will be primarily used to bolster bus service in Seattle.

I believe passing this measure will improve the lives of every Seattleite. I have faith in this prediction as the best predictor of the future is the past, and by every metric, the current STM has been a massive success. It passed in 2020 with a staggering 80% of the vote! But its electoral success does not matter as much as what it actually did . The enormous faith voters placed in the measure has more than paid off, and renewing the measure will continue to build on that momentum. We can see this by breaking down what that money was spent on and what it achieved.

While bus service is provided by King County Metro and thus funded by a county-wide 0.9% sales tax, demand for transit service in Seattle has been higher than the baseline service Metro provides. This is the primary reason why the Seattle Transit Measure was first passed in 2014, passed again overwhelmingly in 2020, and why it should be approved again now.

One out of every 15 buses (approximately 180,000 annual trips) that run in Seattle are currently funded by the STM. That is a massive amount of trips that the STM has delivered every year of its existence.

More buses are better for everyone. For transit riders, increased frequency and reliability means more flexibility and less stress. Frequency is freedom and expanding when and how often a bus runs makes transit more viable as a primary mode of transportation. That makes things better even for drivers as the more people that take the bus– with fewer driving cars, the roads will be safer and less traffic-heavy.

Finally, more transit service is a necessity. From a sustainability standpoint, reducing the total number of vehicles on the road is the single most impactful thing our city can do to reduce its emissions. From a logistics standpoint, the city keeps growing, adding thousands to its population every year. However, we have limited street space. There simply is not room to add more cars to this city at the rate people currently drive. To continue Seattle's growth, we need to make transit a more viable mode of transportation. The current STM has made enormous strides in this regard. Unfortunately, it's still not enough.

Seattle wants more transit service because it needs more transit service. Due to funding issues caused by the Covid-19 pandemic as well as funding and operator availability issues from King County Metro, total bus service is actually at a lower level than it was pre-pandemic in 2019. We are down from 70% of the city having access to ten minute frequency service to approximately 53% . Transit demand has shifted, no longer only commute-based, but also with greater demand being seen for increased frequency on weekends, evenings, and nights. Late night service remains sparse. SDOT's Frequent Transit Network (FTN) , its aspirational goal in service of addressing these shortcomings, is still not fulfilled.

This is where the STM renewal comes into play. The renewal, with its increased funding, will almost double the amount of bus trips added by the current STM, going up to 275,000 trips added annually. It will focus on filling gaps in the FTN, adding additional trips on key routes on off-peak hours. Seattle is a city that does not only exist to go to work and this measure will help make transit a more viable option for every transportation need at all times of the day.

Seattle residents won’t have to wait years to see the benefits. If this measure passes, these additional trips will be phased in relatively quickly as part of Metro's twice-yearly service changes. Metro has confirmed that it is coming out of the operator shortage it has been facing the past few years and stands ready to not only increase its baseline level of service but also fulfill the additional trips that Seattle would be purchasing should STM be renewed. Every additional bus trip funded means that the most affordable transportation option becomes more viable for more people.

It's also important to note that King County Metro, as the operator of the buses, is most directly responsible for safety and security on those buses. By purchasing all this additional bus service, a portion of every transit service purchase goes directly to Metro's safety and security programming. In 2025, 6.3% of STM funds were spent on Metro's safety initiatives. The renewal, by increasing investment in bus service, will continue and expand this investment and continue to make the safest mode of transportation even safer.

On top of bus service, the STM has funding for capital projects to unlock more transit service and make it safer and more reliable. The current STM funded projects such as adding bus lanes on Rainier Ave (which increased performance for riders of the Routes 7, 48, and 106) or contributing funding to the RapidRide J line. While not directly funded by the STM, the recent Denny Way Bus Reliability Project , is another example of the immediate relief that targeted capital projects can provide, having quickly and effectively improved the reliability of both the Route 8 bus. The STM renewal will continue to have funding for capital projects such as these to ensure that buses can run faster, making every dollar invested in transit service go farther.

The current STM also expands access to transit by ensuring that those who need assistance the most can afford to use it. Through the Transportation Access Programs (TAP), STM currently provides around 10,000 free ORCA cards for residents of Seattle Housing Authority, Seattle Promise Scholars, and Seattle Preschool Program families who attend tuition free.

The STM renewal would more than double the amount of ORCA card recipients, going to 22,000 total. While transit is already vastly more affordable than owning and operating a personal car ( which now costs an average annual amount of over twelve thousand dollars nationwide and shows no sign of decreasing, as gas prices continue to climb), there are still many in this city to whom the cost is a barrier. STM and its renewal do not only expand transit, they expand access to transit, which is just as essential.

While buses consist of the majority of transit investments, the STM also funds essential transit services such as the First Hill and South Lake Union Streetcars, Trailhead Direct, and on-demand Metro Flex services.
The STM renewal will continue these investments to ensure that transit access is spread as far as possible.

The STM is a great piece of legislation. It has delivered immediate returns to the taxpayers that overwhelmingly voted it in and its renewal will make its investments even stronger. Investing in stronger, more accessible transit service pays dividends for affordability, safety, livability, and local economy. The more people can afford to safely get where they live and work and play, the better our city becomes.

The impact of an increase to an already high local sales tax cannot be ignored. Unfortunately, until state law changes, sales tax is the most viable method of funding transit service. The STM renewal and its increase of 0.15% to the sales tax rate would be estimated to cost the average Seattle median two-person household an additional $29 per year - even less for many single-person and lower-income households. In an earlier op-ed , the MASS coalition put this cost into context by comparing it to 4 hours of parking, one hour of riding a Lime, a 30 minute uber, a tank of gas, or one week of car ownership.

The purpose of such a comparison is not to make light of what a tax increase means to people at a time where every dollar needs to go the furthest it possibly can. On the contrary, the comparison shows what a good investment the STM renewal truly is and how affordable investment in transit is when compared to other transportation options. If we do not renew the STM, we will face drastic guaranteed transit service cuts. The hit to transit service and the increased cost of relying more on other modes of transportation will far outweigh the cost of the measure.

Seattle is a world-class city with world-class transit, but it can be even better. Good public transit is not free, but it does bring freedom. Freedom to work, to shop, to seek help, to play; freedom from traffic and from never-ending car payments. Transit connects our city and connects people to the places they need to access in order to live their lives.

Sometimes in this city there is a sense that the Seattle Process™ can overwhelm us, slow things down, make it seem like actually changing anything is impossible. That building things is no longer feasible.

We can build, and not only that, we can build quickly and efficiently. Should the STM be renewed, its benefits will not potentially be felt a decade from now. It will be felt within months. Whether you are an avid transit user, driver, both, neither, or anywhere in between, vote Yes on Proposition 1 to renew the Seattle Transit Measure and help build our transit network to make this city more affordable, safe, and easy to navigate.

articles.title: Tom Skerritt Has Left the Grand Illusion
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Tom Skerritt died on October 21 of natural causes. He was 93. I last saw him in 2022 during a dinner party thrown by Michael Hebb on Vashon Island. Low clouds covered that mid-September day, but no rain fell. And Skerritt, who arrived at dusk, sat at the head of a table we shared with the choreographer Donald Byrd. The subject of the night was Generations Over Dinner .

His thoughts were not with the gathering of 10 or so people but somewhere deep within his mind. We spoke a little about this and that. He asked what I was working on, and after I gave him a brief summary of my doings, he politely receded to his thoughts. As the island’s sea-soaked dusk around us grew, and the conversation of human generations (those about to go, those who are new) expanded, Skerritt became more and more pensive. This was not the Skerritt I was accustomed to; the Skerritt who, as an educator and activist for local film production (he moved to the Seattle area in the late ’80s), was committed to everything that had to do with the art of motion pictures, particularly storytelling. This was the substance and vastness of the conversation I had with him in 2018 in a Lower Queen Anne cafe. We talked for nearly two hours, and I left his company feeling a bit special.

Skerritt first came into my world when I was just 10. He had a leading role in a movie, Alien , that, at the time (1979), was reported to be so frightening it caused a person to faint during a screening. More amazing yet, this person had to be carried out of the theater on a stretcher. I had to see this flick, but was prevented from doing so at the box office of a cinema close to my school, Janney Elementary, in Washington, D.C. It was rated R. I wasn’t even close to 17. No can do for you, my guy, said the box office clerk.

I finally watched the movie four years later on a video cassette I rented from a Harare video store (my family returned to Zimbabwe in 1981). And I was drawn not so much by the horror of the alien, which occupied the second part of the film, but the labor disputes that Skerritt’s character, the space-weary Captain Arthur Dallas, had to deal with. My Marxism was born around this time.

A few years after that, I saw Skerritt in the movie Top Gun , which played at a Harare movie theater, Rainbow Cinema. And six years after that (now back in the States), I caught him again in Singles (he played the mayor of Seattle), and also in Contact (he played a government bureaucrat who wasn’t as keen about this alien business as Jodi Foster’s character, Dr. Eleanor Arroway). Of course, these are only a few films in a career that spanned seven decades, and included hits and classics like M*A*S*H , The Dead Zone , Steel Magnolias , and A River Runs Through It . He had a good number of TV shows under his belt, the most noted of which is Picket Fences .

The last movie I saw Skerritt in was East of the Mountains , which my cousin S.J. Chiro directed. Based on a novel of the same name by David Guterson, and released in 2021, the film wasn’t easy to watch because of the directness of its subject and subject matter: an old man, Ben Givens, dealing with death, with personal extinction. As a consequence, Mountain contains moments when the difference between Skerritt and his character seem indistinguishable. Always, the one thing our minds can’t get around, can’t solve, can’t come to terms with is death. How can you be totally something today, and totally nothing tomorrow?

The first time I met Skerritt in person was in 2005, after my film Police Beat screened at SIFF. He attended the movie’s post-show party at Barcça Lounge. He walked through the door, spotted me with a big smile on his face, strided to me, and gave me the biggest hug ever. And he didn’t let go. And all I could think was: I’m finally in Dallas’s arms. Maybe it’s my turn to faint. Goodnight, Skerritt.
The post Tom Skerritt Has Left the Grand Illusion appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: The Garage never should have existed: Why Microsoft’s grassroots innovation lab worked for so long
articles.author: Quinn Hawkins
paras: I saw the news via GeekWire that after 17 years, the Microsoft Garage, which I co-founded, is coming to an end.
In software, 17 years is a very, very long time. I’m proud of how long it lasted.

The funny thing about the Garage is that it never should have existed. When we started it, Microsoft already had bigger, better-funded grassroots innovation programs. And none of us had any idea what we were doing. We’d never built anything like it.
And yet the Garage outlasted all of them. And grew bigger than any of them.
Some of that was luck. But I’d like to believe some of it was smart choices. Here are four that I think mattered, in hopes they help someone else with a similar opportunity.
In case you don’t want to read the whole thing, here’s the short version:
When the Garage started, the other innovation groups at Microsoft had one thing in common. They were built around ideas. Submit an idea. Vote on the ideas. Fund a few winners.
First, it attracted people who liked talking about things more than doing them.

Second, voting doesn’t work. Put ideas to a vote and the obvious ones win. But if an idea is obvious, someone has probably already built it. What you’re really looking for is someone with a special insight. Committees are terrible at spotting special insights.
So the Garage focused on people building small projects. Nobody had to vote. Nobody had to agree. If you wanted to build it, you built it.

That meant someone could build a test tool that made one annoying part of their job easier. Clark Roberts, Victor Boctor, and Mike Cook thought code reviews were too painful, so they co-built CodeFlow as a Garage project. It spread across Microsoft’s development teams and eventually into Visual Studio. Philip Su coded up Dr. Who, the fastest way to look someone up inside the company. Truong Do wanted one mouse and keyboard for all his computers, so he built Mouse Without Borders, which became the first Garage project released to the public.
None of those would have survived a vote. All of them were useful.

It also attracted a certain kind of person. The best coders are often the best because they just love to code. They code all day at work, then go home and code on nights and weekends. Those were Garage people.

Folks like Philip, who went on to be a tech CEO and site lead for Facebook and OpenAI. Vijaye Raji, who built Small Basic as a side project long before he founded Statsig and became CTO of Applications at OpenAI. And the CodeFlow crew: Victor, now a Technical Fellow at Airbnb; Clark, who leads engineering at TaxBit; and Mike, now an engineering leader at Clipboard Health.

As Chris puts it, they fell somewhere between startup founder and safe corporate employee. They wanted the security of a day job and also wanted to chase a dream. No surprise so many went on to do amazing things.
They weren’t interested in sitting around talking about ideas. They wanted to build things that solved their own problems.

It’s also why Ben Gilbert, now of Acquired fame, was the perfect person to take over the Garage after I left. Ben had always been a Garage type of person, building his own iPhone apps on the side. It’s the same doers-not-talkers spirit that led him and David Rosenthal to start hacking on Acquired way back before podcasts had blown up.
The Garage had a tiny budget. Me, one amazing contractor, Liane, and a little money for pizza and poster boards.
Meanwhile, one of the other groups had a chocolate fountain at their event.
Our tiny budget looked like a weakness. It turned out to be one of our biggest assets.

When people asked us to do something, we couldn’t just pay for it. When employees at Microsoft’s Hyderabad campus asked us to put on a science fair, we said: we’d love to support you, but you’ll need to find a way to fund it.
First, it was a great screen. Only the really motivated people made it happen. And when people know they’re expected to lead, they do.
Second, they went to their local leadership and got them to pay for it. And once leadership paid for it, it was their science fair. Not something some outside group was telling them to do.

This happened again and again. Bing wanted a science fair, so Bing sponsored it. The Developer Division wanted one, so DevDiv sponsored it. And because they were paying for it, their leaders wanted it to succeed. They showed up. And each one made the next easier. We could point to a science fair that had worked somewhere else instead of starting cold.

The Garage became something lots of people owned. The well-funded groups never got that. They were islands. Leaders saw them as distractions, and probably a little arrogant for thinking they knew how to innovate.
Turns out a potluck beats a chocolate fountain.
I remember when Steve Ballmer visited Office Labs. Chris Pratley said that after the visit, Steve just asked: “So where’s my next billion-dollar idea?”
That one question explains a lot about why innovation is so hard at big companies.

If you’re an entrepreneur, a business doing $10M, $20M, or $30M a year is a huge success. At Microsoft, it’s a distraction. Big companies are looking for multi-billion-dollar businesses, and they’ll shut down things that are only tens of millions.
So the medium ideas get killed for being too small. And the big ideas need so many resources that they rarely make it either.

The irony is that billion-dollar businesses rarely look like it at the start. Facebook and Twitter didn’t even have a way to make money early on. Demand a path to a billion before you start, and you kill grassroots innovation.

We sidestepped all of that. The Garage was never about finding billion-dollar ideas. It was about supporting people doing grassroots innovation. Helping them build skills, ship things, make friends across the company, and make their own teams better.
Nobody could ask us where the billions were. We never promised any.

People always asked Ben, who ran the Garage after me, “What came out of it?” His answer: mostly culture. And keeping great people at Microsoft who went back to their day jobs re-energized. Look at that list of alumni again. Pretty good return on pizza and poster boards.
One of my favorite Garage stickers said “Do epic shit.” We stole it from J Allard, who’d used it on Xbox.
It was controversial. People worried that a swear word in our materials wouldn’t be appreciated by everybody. They were right. It wasn’t.
But it had a very different energy from the rest of Microsoft. That was the point.

When you’re doing something like this, it helps to step outside the corporate culture and have a little fun. We never wanted to be arrogant. But we did do really fun stuff. Like a giant volcano, built by two pyromaniacs, that got bigger and bolder every time. Or giving people access to a laser cutter with only minimal training.
“Doers, not talkers” had the same tension. People worried it excluded folks who couldn’t code. And honestly, it did. But to have an identity, you have to say what you are and what you aren’t.
When you’re small and scrappy, you have to take risks. And you have to be willing to have an identity that isn’t for everybody.

articles.title: New facility at Washington national lab will give researchers free access to automated tools
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: A first-of-its-kind autonomous research facility is taking shape in central Washington that will provide free access to scientists studying bacteria, yeast and other microorganisms.

The Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) broke ground on the lab, which will open in 2029. PNNL leaders said it will be “one of the world’s largest and most fully autonomous biosciences laboratories” and the first to offer public access through a competitive application process open to U.S. universities, companies and other national laboratories.
The Microbial Molecular Phenotyping Capability (M2PC) is a 30,800-square-foot expansion of the existing Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory on PNNL’s Richland campus.

The new facility will include an integrated system of more than 100 automated instruments that can be programmed to perform laborious research tasks, including growing microbes, measuring their growth and behavior, and linking their genetics and cellular functions to observable traits. Ginkgo Bioworks is supplying the devices.

“M2PC will bring together PNNL’s strengths in microbial science, automation and computing to dramatically accelerate our understanding of what microbes can do and how we put those capabilities to work,” PNNL Director Deb Gracio said in a statement.

The research could address challenges in human health, manufacturing, threat detection, food production and energy. M2PC will also contribute to PNNL’s effort to build computer models that predict and program the behavior of living systems.

The project is part of DOE’s Genesis Mission, which aims to modernize U.S. science through AI and automation. It is funded through the DOE Office of Science’s Biological and Environmental Research program.

articles.title: Watching fruit ripen pays off: Seattle ag-tech startup Strella lands $4.25M
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle-based ag-tech startup Strella has landed $4.25 million to expand the reach of its technology that monitors produce to prevent spoilage and food waste.
The investment extends the company’s Series A round and brings its total funding to $26.25 million.
CEO and co-founder Katherine Sizov launched the startup in Philadelphia in 2019 and relocated its headquarters to Seattle four years ago to be closer to Washington’s fruit orchards.

Strella uses IoT devices to measure gases including ethylene, a plant hormone released by ripening fruit, and machine vision to monitor the produce. Its software interprets the fruit’s real-time conditions alongside data such as country of origin, packing date and varietal type.
The 19-person team serves customers in 26 countries and provides information to growers of apples, pears, avocados and citrus. It recently added kiwifruit to the lineup.
“Our vision is to become the system of record for quality in the food supply chain, or the ‘guardian angels’ of produce as it passes from hand to hand,” Sizov said.
The company works with all of the players in the supply chain, including farmers, produce packers, shippers, distributors and retailers.
“The next step for us is to begin stitching all the pieces together to become a one-stop shop for quality and tackle the food waste problem at scale,” Sizov said.

The United Nations estimates that roughly 33% of food intended for humans worldwide is lost or wasted, totaling $940 billion in annual economic losses. Waste in the U.S. is even worse, at about 40% of edible food and $218 billion each year.
The funding was led by SilverBlue , with participation by LeVert Ventures , Beta Milouot and PeakBridge .

paras: Ballots for the November election have been sent to voters in King County. One item on the ballot for voters in Seattle is Proposition 1: Seattle Transit Measure. This renews and expands the Seattle Transit Measure that is set to expire in early 2027. The 0.3% sales tax is expected to generate $138 million per year that will fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years, 100,000 more bus trips than currently funded. It would also fund 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. Vote Yes to help fund transit in Seattle.

Since 2014, the Seattle Transit Measure has funded millions of bus trips in Seattle. Many of these trips are on weekends when most routes have less frequent service compared to weekdays. Route 36 is one such route that has received additional weekend trips. Between 2022 and 2026, the STM funded 22 additional trips on Saturdays and 42 additional trips on Sunday. In response, more people use Route 36 every weekend. Compared to 2022, Route 36 ridership on Saturday and Sunday has increased by 41% and 58%, respectively. Weekday ridership has increased 32%. This increased ridership represents more car-free trips and improved access to get to work, shops, and fun for people in Beacon Hill, Othello, and the International District.

The Route 36 success story is not an isolated one. Passengers on routes around Seatttle have benefited from additional service funded by the Seattle Transit Measure. Vote Yes to continue and expand the additional bus trips. Fill out your ballot soon and drop it off at one of the many ballot drop boxes in King County.

articles.title: Downtown Highrise Project Still Under Fire as Design Gets Revised Taller
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The property owners behind a potential cross-laminated timber highrise project in Downtown Seattle aren't shirking away in response to considerable pushback against their project – they're going taller. Plans shown this week to the Seattle Landmarks Board would still add a residential tower above a retrofitted Doyle Building at 2nd Avenue and Pine Street, but include six more floors than a proposal initially floated last year .

That change is only likely to intensify opposition to the project, with preservation advocates wary of seeing significant changes to the landmarked 1920 structure joining forces with nearby condo owners not happy about seeing a new tower creep up next door. If built, the new structure would extend 23 stories up alongside its neighbor, the 39-story 1521 2nd Avenue building.

Fana Group, which owns the Doyle Building, has enlisted a team that calls itself Buildings Reimagined – made up of the design firm Clark/Barnes and general contractor BN Builders – to rethink the future of the four-story structure. The Doyle would be converted into a concrete structure capable of supporting a mass-timber tower above, retaining only the north and east facades. A one-story gasket level would accommodate the transition to 18 stories above.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law , Washington cities can no longer require facade modulation or upper level setbacks with mass-timber developments projects or redevelopments that convert commercial space into residential. That means Seattle's existing tower spacing rules do not apply here, with an average distance to the 1521 2nd Avenue building of just under 21 feet. It also means that there are no variances being proposed by Clark/Barnes that could add additional red tape, with the landmarks approval process one of the only remaining barriers standing in the way of potential approval.

"By combining the preservation, the sustainable materials, innovative design, and construction talent, we're going to be able to add more housing downtown," W. Scott Clark of Clark/Barnes told the landmarks board Wednesday. "This is why we created Buildings Reimagined, to help distressed properties that are really challenged and also difficult to entitle, to demonstrate that preservation and financially viable development are not mutually exclusive, and that that they can benefit one another."

Historic preservation advocates apparently disagree. A group called "Save the Historic Doyle Landmark" has already sprouted up to oppose the project as presented, and the advocacy non-profit Historic Seattle sent out an action alert in advance of this week's meeting.

"While not a large or tall structure, the Doyle building has stood out through the decades as downtown has evolved, bearing witness to and surviving the boom-and-bust nature of this city. This human-scale, right-size, mixed-use building stands today due to its original high quality of design, construction, materials, condition, and integrity," Historic Seattle's email stated. "The proposal is to demolish most of the building, leaving only two facades standing, and erecting 23-stories of new residential construction behind the two facades. Let’s be clear. This is NOT an addition to a landmark. This is NOT adaptive reuse. This is NOT historic preservation. This IS facadism. If approved, this would be a demolition of most of the landmark."
But Clark pushed back on claims that they would be demolishing the Doyle this week, framing that as misinformation.

"We are not demolishing the building. We are keeping the two historic featured elevations on the two streets. [...] We are demolishing the alley facade and the roof, and we are going in and we're completely restructuring the interior of this building," Clark said. "Whether you're doing a one-story addition or a taller addition, you would need to reinforce the building to meet seismic. But given the loads that we're going to be subject to, we are going in and we're completely restructuring the internal of the building with a concrete structure."

One point of contention at the Landmarks Board is likely to be the massing of the upper story additions, which are only set back from the Doyle Building's cornices by about three-and-a-half feet. Multiple board members expressed concerns about this, especially as it relates to criteria set by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior on rehabilitation of historic structures. Criteria #9 states that new additions "will be differentiated from the old and will be compatible with the historic materials, features, size, scale and proportion, and massing" compared to the existing structure."

"What I've heard is that this has been scaled and designed to work with economics and making finances work. So as it stands, I have a lot of trouble supporting the project moving forward based on criteria number nine, and seeing that none of that has been applied to this project," board member Matthew Zinski said, referencing the gasket floor intended to be a break between the two segments of building. "Landmarks Board member Matthew Zinski said. "I struggle to see the design logic or what's being used there to help differentiate what's going on between the new addition and the existing building."
Clark defended the choice to extend the addition as far out as it's proposed, noting the limitations that are inherent on the site.

"I do have to say that we were dealing with the reality of a small [floor]plate. It's 8,900 square feet, and secondly, we had to deal with the condition of an eccentric core location, just given the overall dimensions and depths of the plate," Clark said. "We wanted to ensure that our unit layouts had the depth necessary to make comfortable living units, and so all of those things, all those very practical things, in conjunction with the vertical load path that we're trying to run through the building, in coordination with the structure, the existing structure of the landmark building really started to describe the overall mass and form of the building."
Board member Dan Sloat echoed concerns around the addition being too bulky.

"I really appreciate your discussion about the attempt to keep the the new tower structure visually quiet to create that contrast, and I think for me, the kind of equal proportioning of two parts fights against that a little bit," Sloat told Clark. "I'm having a hard time reading the visual quietness of the superstructure because it is so dimensionally similar to the structure below."

Wednesday's briefing, coming more than a year after the firm's first discussion with the Landmarks Board, still represents the early stages of the project. But the design team is heading toward applying for a Master Use Permit with the city, and is advancing forward. In the months ahead it will become clear just how much of an uphill battle getting final approval of the Landmarks Board will be.
But Clark clearly sees the project as a major benefit to downtown Seattle as a whole.

"[The Doyle building] really is at a crossroads, and we think what we're proposing is a very strong, responsible, and reasonable approach to revitalize the building and provide the needed housing downtown," Clark said.

articles.title: New murals bring street art veterans and local roots to five Pike/Pine walls
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Five new murals are now looking out over Pike/Pine, painted by a crew of street art veterans and underground culture builders putting their imprint directly onto Capitol Hill’s everyday walls.

Led by On the Block and the Seattle Artist Coalition for Equitable Development , the “Paint the Block” initiative pulls from “renowned street legends with local longevity and deep neighborhood roots” to turn neighborhood walls into community infrastructure.

The five works span high-traffic corners and quieter stretches. Along the wooden exterior of the Wildrose at 1021 E Pike, Takiyah “TDUB” Ward painted For Shelley, The Wildest Rose honoring the late co-owner of the ‘Rose and urging the neighborhood to “Stay Creative.”
At 1200 E Pine, Myron Curry wrapped the parking bay of NW Liquor in bold scenes of drinks and street life, aiming to “inspire and empower communities through impactful cultural art.”

On a brick wall at 1016 E Pike, project curator Carolyn Hitt joined Maurice “REESBO” Kennedy on Time Traveling , which Kennedy celebrated as a chance to tell their stories in their “own stomping grounds — Capitol Hill.”
A few blocks west at 1426 Boylston Ave, Gerardo “Periko” Peña added a mural of an oversized blue cat Mina lounging among bright red blossoms.

Across from Cal Anderson behind 1535 11th Ave, a massive double piece brings Sam Sneke back to where he says he first “cut my teeth doing graffiti on Capitol Hill” three decades ago, pairing his Welcome to Capitol Hill with Pine Legacy B by SPECSWIZARD , BeSo 206 , and Brandon “ArtbreakerBT” Thomas , all sealed under clear coats brushed on by hip-hop veteran Silas Blak .
Organizers say placing this work front and center sparks foot traffic and safety from the ground up.

“The Seattle underground and behind the scenes is vibrant,” Hitt said. “More resources to these vital culture pockets would go a long way to nurture extraordinary talents that are currently struggling to create under the crushing weight of our economic times.”
Funded by the Seattle Office of Arts and Culture’s HopeCorps under District 3 Councilmember Joy Hollingsworth , the effort is fiscally sponsored by Northwest Film Forum .

Hollingsworth secured $250,000 in JumpStart funds last fall to “support murals in and around Cal Anderson Park” through the HopeCorps program and another $25,000 to fund the painting of the park’s bathroom.
In this year’s budget debate, 19 Capitol Hill and Central District organizations and businesses have joined a call to move $8 million in budget from hiring more cops to spending more on artists.

The mural project also expands on years of DIY work on 11th Ave, growing out of monthly street markets and Eleven:Eleven , the all-ages “little campus of autonomous art studios” opened by On the Block founder Hitt.

Up next, Phase Two of the project will roll out an interactive mobile heritage map on the Capitol Hill Arts District site, followed by artist-led walking tours woven into regular Second Thursday Capitol Hill Art Walks and Second Saturday On the Block markets.

articles.title: Lefty Cheat Sheet: Election choices ‘beyond our two major newspapers’ — and some Seattle left on left political rassling
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Lefty Cheat Sheet at leftycheatsheet.org has arrived as a practical civic utility built to solve one of Seattle’s biggest voter headaches:

Instead of acting like an editorial board that hands down a candidate slate and binary yes-or-no verdicts on ballot measures, the volunteer-run platform functions as an aggregator. Voters can review tracked endorsements across dozens of labor, housing, environmental, and transit advocacy groups, customizing weights and filters to match the specific causes they trust most.

Share The Cities , the group that developed the Lefty Cheat Sheet, describes itself as an all-volunteer Seattle grassroots collective focused on land use, transit, and housing justice and backed by modest community micro-donations. The nonprofit is led by educator and organizer Laura Loe and Kate Rubin, also the co-executive director at Be:Seattle , according to the city. UPDATE : Rubin tells CHS she is no longer part of the leadership of the group.

Naturally, launching an election resource in Seattle’s hyper-charged and robust political left ecosystem brought immediate friction. An independent PAC was blamed for weaponizing the guide in mass campaign texts while taking shots at The Stranger’s ownership changes , forcing the Lefty Cheat Sheet’s volunteer creators to publicly declare their independence. Around the same time, rival political consultants reportedly purchased the .com version of the address to possibly reroute web traffic toward a competing voter guide. UPDATE : One of the consultants involved tells CHS she intended the purchase as an “online joke” and did not intend to use it to redirect voters.
Digital arguments quickly flared over who was genuine and who was attempting to manipulate voters.

Even with the crossfire, the tool’s underlying premise seems like it could hold. Rather than relying on top-down decrees from legacy institutions or wading through endless social media spats, Seattle voters might have gained an adaptable way to more carefully decide their ballots.
You can find the cheat sheet at leftycheatsheet.org .

articles.title: Seattle councilmember proposes new rules to curb long-term budget deficits
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: As Seattle tries to tackle an estimated $175 million budget deficit, citywide Councilmember Dionne Foster has proposed two new fiscal sustainability measures designed to curb recurring, multi-year shortfalls.

The proposed legislation would establish accountability standards for both the executive and legislative branches at Seattle City Hall. Under the proposals, the mayor’s office would be mandated to submit balanced future-year financial plans for both the General Fund and the JumpStart Payroll Expense Tax Fund. In addition, the Seattle City Council would be required to ensure its final, adopted budgets maintain balanced projections over that same timeline.

The package builds upon voter-approved 2025 “Seattle Shield” legislation that cut B&O for small businesses, boosted taxes on large corporations like Amazon and Starbucks and required balanced out-year projections through 2030, but only applied that standard to the 2027 budget. Foster’s proposal aims to make multi-year fiscal discipline a permanent governing rule.

In her announcement, Foster said that the city can no longer balance its ledger year-to-year while leaving downstream deficits to future leaders. Fellow councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Eddie Lin have voiced their support.
The council will review the proposals during budget briefings starting October 27th, with a public hearing on the 2027-2028 budget scheduled for November 5th.

articles.title: Idaho Lawmakers Tried to Conflate Abortion with Human Trafficking and Seattle Attorneys Are Fighting Back
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: Three years ago, the Idaho state legislature passed a law making it illegal to assist minors in crossing state lines to access abortion care. In the paranoiac tradition of American anti-abortion policy, the law was rooted in a poorly disguised moral panic : It specifically banned “abortion trafficking”—the fictional concept of shadowy adults coercing minors into having abortions and abducting them to make it happen. This, obviously, is a problem that doesn’t exist, and would curtail the very real rights of minors and their allies, all while claiming to have children’s best interests at heart.

Now, a lawsuit spearheaded by the Seattle-based gender equality legal advocacy group Legal Voice is challenging Idaho’s law, and what comes next could impact access to abortion everywhere, for better or for worse. “Everyone wants young people to be healthy and safe, but this law, if it stands, will put them in danger and isolate them from trusted adults, which is what nobody wants,” says Wendy Heipt, senior litigation counsel at Legal Voice.

Idaho has a trigger law that immediately criminalized abortion when Roe v. Wade was overturned, but Idahoans seeking abortions commonly travel to states like Washington and Oregon for care, a dynamic that predates Roe ’s reversal and has stymied the efforts of anti-abortion activists, since freedom of movement is a constitutionally protected right. But by targeting young people’s access to abortion, Idaho lawmakers may have identified a loophole in their efforts to curtail abortion-related travel, one likely to be replicated elsewhere if it’s allowed to continue.

Legal Voice is arguing that Idaho’s travel ban blocks the First Amendment by preventing Idahoans from even discussing abortions across state lines. The law is also poorly written: it states that it’s illegal for an adult to “harbor” or “recruit” minors, but doesn’t give clear definitions for either term, which creates confusion both about following and enforcing the law. And then there’s that one pesky detail in the Constitution: the right to travel between states is a fundamental personal freedom, one that states with anti-abortion policies have struggled to successfully undermine, even as restrictive abortion bans have gone into effect since Roe v. Wade was overturned.

In an April memorandum requesting a summary judgment in the case, attorneys from Legal Voice, the Lawyering Project, and Stoel Rives LLP mapped out concerns the law raises about barring travel tied to health care when that treatment is legal in the destination state. “If states could prohibit such assistance, the right to travel would become meaningless in practice,” they wrote.
But if Legal Voice’s case prevails, it could set a useful precedent by affirming that an anti-abortion policy in one state can’t necessarily be enforced in another.

So far, Legal Voice and the case plaintiffs have secured an injunction to keep the law from going into effect. It was modified following an appeal to the Ninth Circuit and remains partially in place. Still, according to Legal Voice, “Under the current order, our clients can still provide information, encouragement, and financial resources to youth seeking abortion care.” Now back at the district court level, both sides have issued motions for a summary judgment, meaning a ruling could soon be issued, without the need for a trial.

Legal Voice’s plaintiffs in the case are Lourdes Matsumoto, a lawyer who needs to freely share abortion information in her work with young survivors of sexual assault and domestic violence; the Northwest Abortion Access Fund; and the Indigenous Idaho Alliance, which works with five Northwest tribes and connects pregnant people with abortion resources. “They serve indigenous communities throughout Idaho, including for health care autonomy, and they want to support people making their own decisions, including minors,” says Heipt. “And their family structure doesn’t always fit the way the laws are written.”

In choosing to target young people and the adults who support them, Idaho’s law isn’t unusual. It’s a common tactic in anti-abortion legislation (and anti-trans legislation, for that matter; the two are irrevocably intertwined ): Work your way up to targeting access to health care for everyone, but begin by eroding minors’ access. “That’s typically where it starts,” says Heipt. “If they are successful with minors, I can assure you that it will not stop with minors.”

Historically, anti-abortion activists have accomplished this through policies like parental notification laws, popularized even before the US Supreme Court overturned Roe in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization . These laws required minors to involve their parents in decisions about abortion, or to make their case before a judge to get permission if involving a parent wasn’t possible.
Though it contains no real requirements for involvement from a caregiver, Idaho’s abortion travel ban has been justified, like parental notification laws, as a policy promoting parental rights.

But just as “abortion trafficking” isn’t a real problem, a parental rights framing around abortion doesn’t make much sense, either, since data shows most young people who seek abortion care voluntarily choose to involve trusted family members.

A study on parental involvement in minors’ abortion decisions, published in the Journal of Adolescent Health , found that most minors—64 percent—specifically shared their plans to seek abortion care with their mothers, and, intriguingly, that parental involvement did not automatically equate to greater confidence in pregnancy decisions. Even without parental support, 81 percent of young people had “high confidence” in their own decision-making around abortion; maternal involvement was “not significantly associated with having high confidence in the decision,” the researchers found.

This is a very different reality than the “abortion trafficking” Idaho’s travel ban has purported to solve. In fact, when the law was first introduced in the Idaho legislature, Idaho Anti-Trafficking Coalition executive director Jennifer Zielinski told the Idaho Statesman that conflating human trafficking with helping someone voluntarily seeking abortion disrupted actual efforts to stop trafficking and risked retraumatizing victims. While human trafficking does sometimes involve forced abortion or pregnancy as a tool of control, the Idaho law would do nothing to help. “It takes the true effort off course,” Zielinski told the paper.

Heipt agrees. “It really does a disservice to actual survivors of trafficking to call something ‘trafficking’ because you don’t like it,” she says. And even the bill’s proponents seemed to understand this: The word “trafficking” has since been removed from the law, a nod to its bad-faith framing.
Whether a judge will view it that way remains to be seen. A decision in the case is expected early next year.

paras: Train kills man in wheelchair: Moments before a BNSF freight train hurtled through a downtown Puyallup crossing, a couple in a car noticed a man in an electric wheelchair stuck trying to cross the tracks. A man jumped out of the car, tried to lift the wheelchair from the tracks, and, when that didn’t work, attempted to free the man from his seatbelt. The train came too fast. It struck and killed the man in the wheelchair.

One year with the use of force tool: Last year, the Washington Data Exchange for Public Safety ( WADEPS ), a tool that tracks police use of force statewide, launched. If you’ve ever wanted to see how our police departments behave, now you can. This year, according to WADEPS, there have been 1,200 uses of force statewide. KING5 reports that these range from police “shootings to police releasing a police dog on a subject.” Eight people have died from use of force this year and there have been no officers disciplined. Only about 80 percent of the 218 departments in the state have their data represented here, though they’re all required to do so. Reports can also be inconsistent depending on the month.

Suspicious: Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy group, wants answers . Last Saturday, during the No Kings March, Meta allegedly suspended the official No Kings Instagram account. Public Citizen has filed a Freedom of Information Act request to get to the bottom of the block.

Trump supports that terrible Ramaswamy ad: This week, Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy funded an attack ad on his Democrat opponent, Amy Acton. The ad features Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar, saying Acton has “serious problems with the truth.” Acton has not seen her mother since 1978, when she testified against her stepfather for physically and sexually abusing her and her brother for years. She was 12. Many people—even Republicans—have denounced the ad, calling it a real low even for modern politics. Not Trump or his camp. Trump called it “powerful” and told Ramaswamy he should thank God for the ad.

German far-right party has been wooing Trump for a decade: Not to steal Hunter’s thunder, but here is some Nazi news.
